newsitem.title: PERU: Peru says progress in rebel talks, problems remain.
newsitem.headline: Peru says progress in rebel talks, problems remain.

text.p: Peru's President Alberto Fujimori said on Thursday the government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages were making progress toward ending the 100-day crisis but there were still problems to overcome.

The men held at the Japanese ambassador's home are set to spend the Easter holiday under the gun, but the final negotiating phase seems likely to start early next week. "Even though, naturally, difficulties still exist, we are getting closer," Fujimori told local television station Panamericana.

The president boosted growing optimism in Lima that a solution to the siege was in sight. He said he was confident the energetic work of the talks guarantors, hammering out a deal acceptable to both sides, "is going to bear fruit".

A Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) military leader in Peru's central jungle agreed the sides were getting closer but said the government still had to come up with a satisfactory offer to meet their demand for the freedom of jailed comrades.
"The sides are getting closer but the main demand for the release of prisoners still has to be addressed," Comrade Alejandro told Reuters from the jungle. He did not elaborate.

In a four-point statement read by the hostage-takers' second-in-command inside the residence, Rolly Rojas, the MRTA said a "peaceful solution for the crisis is in the government's hands and will come about if they address our demands."
In a walkie-talkie interview with Reuters, the rebel negotiator also dismissed as "pure speculation" local media reports detailing a deal purportedly made by the two sides.
The MRTA originally demanded freedom for up to 450 prisoners but spokesmen have said the group was willing to negotiate a reduced number if the freed comrades were high-ranking fighters.
Fujimori has consistently rejected the release of any MRTA member, but speculation has been rife in diplomatic and media circles that he was ready to free some low-ranking members.

This issue was likely to be the most contentious point when talks resume. There is no date for a resumption of talks -- on hold since March 12 -- but the face-to-face meeting was expected to take place on Monday or Tuesday.

"We hope that very soon the government's representative, (Education) Minister (Domingo) Palermo, can hold a meeting," Fujimori said. "We have concluded the stage of preliminary conversations and, even if we have not yet started the final conversations, we have an interval for reflection. Easter is just right for that."

One part of a deal to end Latin America's longest hostage siege appears to be set -- asylum in Cuba for the hostage-takers. Diplomats say the rebels have accepted Havana's offer of safe haven and MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco said this week they would take asylum as part of a deal that included the freeing of some jailed comrades.
While the rebels and Fujimori were moving closer together, Fujimori hinted there were still some differences between Tokyo and Lima on how to end the crisis.

"Perhaps we live the situation here more intimately. In Japan, despite the media, there is a distance that does not allow a precise perception of what is going on and what might happen," Fujimori said.

The Peruvian leader said he interrupted a cabinet meeting for 50 minutes late on Wednesday to discuss the siege by telephone with Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto. Local media reported Hashimoto had used the conversation to press for Peru to allow some releases of jailed MRTA members.
